body:
The emergence of large territorial states

During the 6th century BCE, northern India experienced an important political change. Smaller settlements and kingdoms gradually developed into larger territorial states. Competition for fertile land, agricultural produce, trade routes and military resources encouraged rulers to extend their authority over neighbouring territories.

The term janapada literally means the land on which a jana, or people, established itself. A mahajanapada was a larger and more powerful territorial state. Buddhist and Jain traditions refer to 16 mahajanapadas, including Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, Avanti, Gandhara and Vajji.

Not every mahajanapada had the same political system. Many were monarchies governed by kings. Others, including Vajji, followed a gana-sangha system in which authority was shared by a group of ruling members. These assemblies were not modern democracies because participation was restricted.

Why larger states needed greater resources

As territories expanded, rulers needed soldiers, officials, fortifications and arrangements for transporting supplies. Occasional gifts from subjects were insufficient for these continuing expenses. Consequently, rulers increasingly depended on regular taxation.

In the mahajanapada period, taxes were collected from different economic activities:

  • Agriculture: Crop taxes were particularly important because most people depended on farming. A commonly mentioned share was 1/6 of agricultural produce, known as bhaga.
  • Craft production: Artisans could provide goods, labour or other contributions.
  • Animal husbandry: Herders supplied animals or animal products.
  • Trade: Goods bought and sold could be taxed.
  • Forests: Forest communities could supply valuable forest products.

The agricultural share of 1/6 is a general textbook description of taxation in the mahajanapada period. It should not be treated as proof that every Mauryan province subsequently paid an identical rate.

Some rulers also maintained standing armies: soldiers who served regularly and were supported by the state rather than being assembled only for individual campaigns.

Revenue and military strength were connected. Taxes helped maintain armies, while armies protected territories and enabled further expansion.

Why Magadha became the strongest mahajanapada

Between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE, Magadha emerged as the most powerful mahajanapada. Its rise resulted from a combination of geographical advantages, economic resources and political expansion.

Fertile agricultural land

Magadha occupied an advantageous position in the eastern Gangetic plains, principally in present-day Bihar. Fertile soil and dependable water supplies supported agricultural production. The increasing use of iron ploughshares and transplantation of paddy in suitable areas helped increase yields.

Greater agricultural production supported a larger population and provided resources that rulers could collect through taxation.

Rivers and communication

The Ganga, Son and other rivers facilitated transportation, communication and the movement of goods. River transport was particularly valuable for moving bulky agricultural produce and maintaining links between settlements.

Iron and forest resources

Accessible iron deposits in the adjoining region of present-day Jharkhand supported the production of agricultural tools and weapons. Forests supplied timber and elephants. Elephants were particularly valuable for warfare, while timber was useful for buildings, carts and military equipment.

Political leadership and expansion

Bimbisara and Ajatashatru were important early rulers who strengthened Magadha through conquest and political alliances. Bimbisara is associated with the conquest of Anga. Ajatashatru continued expansion and is particularly associated with conflict against the Vajji confederacy.

Magadha's early capital was Rajagriha, also called Rajagaha, identified with present-day Rajgir in Bihar. It was a fortified settlement surrounded by hills.

During the 4th century BCE, the capital was shifted to Pataliputra, present-day Patna. Its advantageous position on important river routes helped rulers supervise communication, trade and territorial administration.

The central relationship: Productive agriculture and natural resources helped Magadha collect revenue and maintain armies. Military power and effective communication then supported further territorial expansion.

Prelims focus

  • Janapada means the settled territory of a people; mahajanapada refers to a larger territorial state.
  • Magadha was located mainly in present-day Bihar.
  • Rajagriha was Magadha's earlier capital; Pataliputra became its later capital.
  • Bimbisara and Ajatashatru were important rulers during Magadha's expansion.
  • The Ganga river system, fertile land, iron and elephants contributed to Magadha's strength.
  • Trap: Vajji was associated with a gana-sangha, whereas Magadha developed as a powerful monarchy.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 6, Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic, printed pp. 57–61, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 29–31.]

title: From Janapadas to Magadha: The Foundations of Territorial Expansion

body:
The Nandas and the expansion of Magadha

The Nanda dynasty ruled Magadha during the 4th century BCE, immediately before the establishment of the Mauryan Empire. It followed the Shishunaga dynasty and inherited a state that had already become powerful through agriculture, taxation, military organisation and territorial conquest.

The Nandas expanded this political foundation. Their rule is associated with extensive territorial authority, a substantial treasury and a powerful army. They therefore occupy an important position between the earlier mahajanapada kingdoms and the much larger Mauryan Empire.

Mahapadma Nanda and territorial expansion

Mahapadma Nanda is generally identified as the founder and most important early ruler of the Nanda dynasty. He is credited with expanding Magadha's authority over several older kingdoms and ruling families.

Later traditions describe him as ekarat, meaning a sole or paramount ruler. This reflects his reputation for bringing previously separate territories under one political authority.

Accounts of his conquests associate Nanda power with territories beyond the original Magadhan heartland, including expansion towards the north-west. However, the exact extent of Nanda territory cannot be established with the same confidence as the broad distribution of the later Mauryan Empire.

The important development was the consolidation of a large territorial kingdom that extended beyond the older political boundaries of Magadha.

Revenue collection and the Nanda army

The Nandas are particularly associated with wealth, systematic revenue collection and military strength.

A large army required continuous expenditure on soldiers, animals, weapons, equipment and supplies. Revenue from agricultural production, commerce and other taxable activities provided the economic resources needed to sustain this establishment.

The Nanda state is associated with more systematic collection of revenue through appointed officials. This strengthened the ability of the ruler to draw resources from a large territory.

Greek accounts describe the Nanda military establishment as exceptionally large. Ancient estimates include substantial numbers of infantry, cavalry, chariots and war elephants. Such numerical claims should not be treated as verified military counts; their principal significance is that contemporaries regarded the kingdom as a formidable military power.

A large army was not merely a result of territorial expansion. It also helped rulers defend existing territories, suppress opposition and undertake further campaigns. Revenue and military power strengthened each other.

Dhana Nanda and the end of the dynasty

Dhana Nanda is traditionally identified as the last Nanda ruler. His reign is associated with considerable wealth and military strength.

Later historical and literary traditions also portray Nanda taxation as burdensome and Dhana Nanda as unpopular. These accounts help explain the traditional narrative of his overthrow, but their descriptions of his character and the scale of taxation are not independently established contemporary facts.

By approximately 322–321 BCE, Chandragupta Maurya had replaced Nanda rule in Magadha and established the Mauryan dynasty.

Alexander and the north-western frontier

While the Nandas ruled Magadha, Alexander of Macedonia campaigned in the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent.

In 326 BCE, Alexander's forces advanced into the Punjab region. After campaigning there, his army reached the Beas River, where the soldiers refused to proceed farther east.

The refusal followed prolonged military campaigning and exhaustion. Reports about powerful Indian armies, including large forces with war elephants farther east, also contributed to the reluctance to continue.

Alexander consequently did not march into Magadha and did not defeat the Nanda rulers.

Alexander's withdrawal and the subsequent weakening of Macedonian authority in parts of the north-west created political opportunities that Chandragupta Maurya later exploited.

Two separate developments

Alexander's campaign concerned the north-western frontier, whereas Nanda rule was centred on Magadha in the eastern Gangetic plains. The Macedonian army did not conquer the Nanda capital at Pataliputra.

Transition from Nanda to Mauryan rule

Chandragupta did not begin with an entirely undeveloped kingdom. The Nandas had already consolidated considerable territory and resources. Chandragupta took control of this established political base and subsequently expanded Mauryan power much farther.

Prelims focus

  • The Nanda dynasty ruled Magadha during the 4th century BCE.
  • Mahapadma Nanda is associated with extensive territorial expansion.
  • Dhana Nanda was the last Nanda ruler.
  • The Nandas were known for considerable revenue resources and military strength.
  • Alexander's soldiers refused to proceed beyond the Beas River in 326 BCE.
  • Trap: Alexander did not conquer Magadha or overthrow Dhana Nanda. Chandragupta Maurya replaced Nanda rule.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 6, printed pp. 60–61; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed p. 31; Suchandra Ghosh, Nanda Empire, The Encyclopedia of Empire, 2016, abstract, Wiley Online Library, consulted 18 November 2026; P. Bhaskar Reddy, Mahajanapadas–Rise of Magadha–Nandas–Invasion of Alexander, Outlines of Indian History, sections 5.3 and 7, INFLIBNET, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Alexander's advance stopped at the Beas, far to the north-west of Magadha.

title: The Nanda Dynasty: Revenue, Military Power and Pre-Mauryan Expansion

body:
Foundation of the Mauryan Empire

Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire around 321 BCE, establishing a new dynasty after the overthrow of the Nandas.

The new empire was centred on Pataliputra, the established political centre of Magadha. Its location in the Gangetic plains allowed Chandragupta to benefit from the agricultural resources, established settlements and communication routes of the earlier kingdom.

Chandragupta is traditionally associated with Chanakya, also known as Kautilya, who is remembered as his adviser and an important figure in early Indian political thought.

Chanakya and the Arthashastra

The Arthashastra is a major work associated with Kautilya. It discusses important aspects of statecraft, including administration, taxation, intelligence, military organisation and relations between states.

The association between Chandragupta and Chanakya is a well-established historical tradition. However, the surviving Arthashastra is a text with a complex history of composition. It should not be assumed that every passage in its present form was personally written by Chanakya during Chandragupta's reign.

Expansion towards the north-west

One of Chandragupta's major achievements was the extension of Mauryan authority across northern India and towards the north-western frontier.

Following Alexander's death in 323 BCE, the territories formerly controlled by his empire were contested by his successors. Chandragupta strengthened his position in the north-west and eventually came into conflict with Seleucus I Nicator, a successor of Alexander who controlled important territories in West Asia.

The agreement with Seleucus

The conflict was followed by a diplomatic settlement, generally dated to approximately 305–303 BCE.

Under the settlement, Seleucus relinquished claims to territories towards the north-western frontier, including areas associated with present-day Afghanistan and Baluchistan. Chandragupta's control was thereby extended towards the Hindu Kush region.

Ancient accounts record that Seleucus received 500 war elephants in connection with the agreement. Diplomatic relations subsequently developed between the Seleucid and Mauryan courts.

The precise boundaries covered by the settlement are not completely certain. Its central historical importance is the consolidation of Mauryan authority in the north-west and the establishment of diplomatic relations with a major Hellenistic power.

Megasthenes and the Mauryan court

Megasthenes was a Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus to Chandragupta's court.

He visited the Mauryan Empire and wrote an account generally known as Indica. Although the complete original work has not survived, portions are preserved through later Greek and Roman writers.

Megasthenes described Pataliputra, the royal establishment and aspects of Mauryan administration. His account is especially useful for understanding how the large empire functioned during Chandragupta's period.

Correct association: Chandragupta Maurya was the founder of the dynasty; Chanakya or Kautilya was traditionally his adviser; Seleucus I Nicator was the Hellenistic ruler associated with the north-western settlement; and Megasthenes was the Greek ambassador who visited Chandragupta's court.

Bindusara: The second Mauryan emperor

Bindusara succeeded his father Chandragupta Maurya around 298 BCE and ruled until approximately 273 BCE, according to a commonly used chronology.

He inherited a substantial empire extending well beyond the original territory of Magadha. His reign was important for maintaining this large political structure and continuing relations with neighbouring Hellenistic rulers.

Bindusara is sometimes associated with the title Amitraghata, meaning destroyer of enemies. Greco-Roman references use the related name Amitrochates.

Later traditions credit Bindusara with territorial expansion into parts of the Deccan. However, the available evidence does not securely establish the precise extent or chronology of these conquests. It is therefore safer to identify him primarily as the ruler who maintained and consolidated the empire inherited from Chandragupta, while recognising that further expansion may have occurred.

His successor was his son Ashoka, who became the third major ruler of the Mauryan dynasty.

Why the transition mattered

The first 2 Mauryan generations established a durable imperial framework. Chandragupta acquired Magadha's established resources and extended territorial control. Bindusara maintained the larger political structure. Ashoka subsequently inherited an empire with established administrative centres, military resources and communication networks.

Prelims focus

  • Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire around 321 BCE.
  • Chanakya and Kautilya are names associated with Chandragupta's adviser.
  • The agreement with Seleucus I Nicator is generally dated to 305–303 BCE.
  • Megasthenes visited Chandragupta's court and wrote Indica.
  • Bindusara was Chandragupta's son and Ashoka's father.
  • Trap: Extensive Deccan conquests under Bindusara are described in later traditions but are not securely established in detail.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, Ashoka, the Emperor Who Gave Up War, printed pp. 75–78; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed pp. 32–33; P. Bhaskar Reddy, The Mauryan Empire, Outlines of Indian History, sections 4, 5.1 and 5.2, INFLIBNET, consulted 18 November 2026.]
